hook_text: In 1955, a whole neighbourhood full of jazz, writers and families was wiped off the map and given a new name: Triumph.
clip_script: Sophiatown, Johannesburg, in the early 1950s. Crowded, poor, and full of life. Jazz in the shebeens. Writers at Drum magazine. And something rare: black families who owned their own homes. Then came the Group Areas Act, colouring in every town by race. Sophiatown had to go. The people answered: We won't move. Before dawn on 9 February 1955, in pouring rain, about two thousand armed police arrived. Families were loaded onto trucks with everything they owned and driven to Meadowlands. Over the next years, every house was bulldozed. On the ruins, the government built a white suburb and named it Triomf. Triumph. It happened again in District Six, in Cato Manor, in South End. Millions moved. In 2006, Sophiatown got its name back.
visual_style: Black-and-white photographs of Sophiatown streets and jazz musicians; a Drum magazine cover; a 'We won't move' slogan painted on a wall; police trucks in the rain; bulldozers demolishing houses; rows of identical Meadowlands houses; a modern Sophiatown street sign.
mood: Nostalgic, then heartbreaking, then quietly defiant.
pacing: Lively at the start, sudden and heavy at the removal, slow at the end.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to learn about the Group Areas Act and the destruction of Sophiatown.
